title: Stay with the Lord, my mind
hook: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: stay always with the Lord and your troubles will pass (Anand 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, and your line, joy, mother. Did you share some good news? Today, pauri two, where the Guru talks to his own mind. Day three hundred eighty-three.

Do you talk to yourself? Plenty of people do, even if they'd never admit it. Come on. Focus. Don't check the phone. You've got this. Some of it is harsh, the inner voice that sounds like a bad coach. Some of it is kinder. Either way, the mind needs reminding, again and again, of what it already knows, because it wanders off the moment you stop watching it. The second pauri of Anand Sahib is the Guru talking to his own mind. Not to a crowd. Not even to God, exactly. To himself. Today: man meriaa.
screen: `EVERYONE TALKS TO THEMSELVES.` → `THE MIND NEEDS REMINDING.` → `THE GURU TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, transliterated: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale. O my mind, always stay with the Lord. Man is the mind, the restless inner self. Meriaa: my. Sadaa: always. Har naale: with the Lord, alongside. Then, in paraphrase: stay with the Lord, my mind, and all your pains will be forgotten. He will take you as his own, and set all your affairs right. The Master can do all things; why forget him from your mind? And it ends where it began: says Nanak, my mind, always stay with the Lord. Notice the tone. It's not scolding. It's the voice of someone who has just found joy in pauri one, turning to his own wandering mind and saying, stay. Don't drift off now. Naale is a lovely little word. It's beside, alongside, the word you'd use for walking with a friend. Not under. Not far above. With. And notice the promise is about the pains being forgotten, not about them never happening. The troubles are real. In the pauri, staying beside the Lord is what loosens their grip. Angeekaar, the word for being taken as his own, is the same idea you met in Chaupai: being claimed, held, adopted. And then that gentle question: why forget him? Not a threat. Almost puzzled. If the Master can do everything, why would you wander off? It's the question you'd ask a friend who keeps wandering off from the one person who always shows up for them. That's the second pauri. The joy has come. Now the work is to stay with it.
screen: `AE MAN MERIAA: O MY MIND.` · `NAALE: ALONGSIDE, LIKE A FRIEND.` · `THE PAINS FORGOTTEN, NOT ABSENT.` · `WHY FORGET HIM? NOT A THREAT.` · then, large: `STAY WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with one thing. For the next two minutes, choose one simple thing to stay with: your breath, a candle, the sound of a fan, a word like Waheguru if you pray. Every time your mind wanders off, and it will, gently bring it back, the way the pauri does. No scolding. Just: stay. Count how many times you return, if that helps. Then, later today, try it for five whole minutes with something ordinary: washing dishes, a walk, a cup of tea. Stay with that one thing the whole way through. The bell holds the time.
Man meriaa, O my mind. Ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: the Guru telling his own mind, gently, to stay beside the Lord, and the pains will loosen.
Your line: stay with him. Today, whenever you notice your mind has wandered off, say to it, kindly, the way you'd talk to a friend: stay. Day three hundred eighty-three.

screen: `DAY 383 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOUR HOUSE DOESN'T HOLD.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this second pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and the opening line is often quoted as a reminder to keep the mind with God through the day.

pairs: the mind, the restless inner self

myth: pauri two is addressed to a crowd
ae man meriaa: it's addressed to the Guru's own mind.
the pauri says staying with the Lord means troubles never happen
it says the pains will be forgotten, their grip loosened, not that they never come.
naale means alongside, the way you'd walk with a friend
not under or far above: with.

fork.setup: you've just found joy, and already your mind is wandering off to the next worry. what does pauri two say to it?
options: scold it harshly until it obeys.
O my mind, always stay with the Lord.
let it wander; it doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: O my mind, always stay with the Lord. said gently, with a puzzled question: why forget him?

original.note: Gurmukhi: man meriaa, O my mind, the address that opens Anand Sahib's second pauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: an instruction to think about God all day.
what it means: the Guru gently telling his own wandering mind to stay alongside the Lord, so the pains loosen their grip.
what a scholar hears: Anand repeatedly addresses the man, the mind, in the vocative 'ae man meriaa', making much of the bani an inner dialogue.

sources.quoted: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale

notes: Transliteration as in the index; pauri 2 paraphrased ('har naal rahu too man mere dookh sabh visaaranaa; angeekaar oh kare teraa kaaraj sabh savaaranaa; sabhnaa galaa samrath suaamee so kio manahu visaare'). Confirm.
Angeekaar glossed as 'take as his own'; linked to Chaupai's 'apnaa jaan'. Confirm.
The claim that Anand repeatedly addresses the mind (several pauris begin 'ae man') is in the trapdoor. Confirm.
The outline practice is 'stay with one thing for five minutes'; the sit is two minutes, so the practice does two now and invites five later.
Editor review (2026-10-01): the claim that staying with the Lord loosens pain is now the pauri's, not the narrator's; replaced the child-in-a-crowd image, which repeated day 377's hook.
